items.prompt: What is subtext?
choices: A written summary of everything that was said aloud
The real message under or instead of the words
The main point made by the loudest speaker
items.explanation: Subtext is the message conveyed beneath or in place of the literal words.

items.prompt: What is a transcript?
choices: The hidden message behind what people said
The literal words that were spoken aloud
A guess about what everyone really wants
items.explanation: A transcript is only the literal words, nothing inferred.

items.prompt: What is an unstated agenda?
choices: A schedule printed before the meeting starts
A goal someone holds but does not say aloud
A topic the whole group agreed to cover
items.explanation: An unstated agenda is a goal that shapes responses without being spoken.

items.prompt: What does it mean that someone has something at stake?
choices: They are sitting closest to the screen
They could gain, lose, or protect something
They happened to speak first in the meeting
items.explanation: Stakes are what a person stands to gain, lose, protect, or be blamed for.

items.prompt: Four friends say 'fine' and a fifth says nothing. How should the silence be treated?
choices: As proof the fifth friend is angry
As a clue worth a gentle question
As agreement with the other four
items.explanation: A missing reaction is a clue, so you ask; it is not proof of anything.

items.prompt: Which description fits a clue best?
choices: A confirmed fact about what someone thinks
A reason to ask a careful question first
A rumor you can safely pass to others
items.explanation: A clue justifies asking. It does not confirm a motive.

items.prompt: Which of these can you quote word for word?
choices: The subtext
The transcript
The unstated agenda
items.explanation: Only the spoken words can be quoted exactly; the rest is inferred.

items.prompt: A friend says 'fine' but sighs and looks away. What is a sensible first move?
choices: Tell the others they are secretly upset about it
Ask them privately if something is bothering them
Ignore the sigh and carry on exactly as before
items.explanation: Asking turns the clue into information without accusing anyone.

items.prompt: Everyone at dinner says 'fine, anywhere works' and the usual first suggester says nothing. Which statement is most defensible?
choices: The silent friend is clearly angry and wants a different restaurant instead
The words show no objection, and the missing reaction is a clue to ask about
The group agreed, because no one objected out loud during the discussion
Nothing can be learned, because silence never carries any information at all
items.explanation: The words contain no objection, but the break in a known pattern is a clue to check. It proves neither anger nor agreement, and silence is not automatically meaningless.
items.reference:
What is said versus what is meant
📝 Transcript: the literal words, quotable
🧭 Subtext: the real message, only inferable
⚠️ A clue prompts a question and never proves a motive
Why: the words and the message can differ, and a clue only justifies asking, never concluding.
items.learnMore:
Subtext is inferred, so hold it loosely

A transcript can be quoted word for word. Subtext cannot; it is read from who reacted, who did not, and what each person has at stake. Because it is inferred, it can be wrong.

Common mistake

Treating an inference about someone's motive as a fact you can repeat.
items.reflection: Think of a conversation where the words were fine but you left unsure. What clue made you doubt them, and how could you have checked it?

items.prompt: Why can two accurate recordings of one meeting lead to different understandings of it?
choices: One of the two recordings must have missed some of the spoken words
Recordings capture the subtext of a meeting in full when they are accurate
Accuracy covers the words, while the message depends on the reactions
Understanding is always decided by whoever happened to speak the loudest
items.explanation: A recording is a transcript. The message also lives in who reacted, who stayed quiet, and what each person had at stake, none of which words alone settle.

items.prompt: After a budget cut a manager says 'I trust your judgment.' Which reading respects 'a clue is not proof'?
choices: It proves they will blame you if the work goes badly later on
It is only a compliment and carries no other message to consider
It means the budget cut no longer affects the plans you made
It might signal pressure, so ask what limits they have in mind
items.explanation: The timing is a clue that more may be meant, so the honest move is to ask. Claiming blame is certain, or that nothing is meant, both skip the check.

items.prompt: Which phrase is a hedge?
choices: The deadline is Friday
I disagree with step two
Let's take it offline
items.explanation: A hedge sounds mild and commits to nothing, like 'let's take it offline'.

items.prompt: What does hedge language usually avoid?
choices: Every mention of the topic at all
Speaking in a calm and level voice
Both agreeing and disagreeing openly
items.explanation: Hedges let a person skip committing to either side.

items.prompt: Which is the other common carrier of subtext, besides hedges?
choices: A loud argument between two other people
A printed agenda that is sent in advance
Silence from someone who usually reacts
items.explanation: A missing expected reaction is the second carrier.

items.prompt: 'Worth exploring' is best described as what?
choices: A firm approval to start building it
A direct refusal of the whole idea
Mild interest that commits to nothing
items.explanation: It sounds positive but promises nothing concrete.

items.prompt: What does 'reading the room' compare?
choices: How many people attended against room size
The meeting length against the planned length
What was said against who reacted and who did not
items.explanation: It compares the words with the reactions and the stakes.

items.prompt: Why does a transcript hide hedges and silences?
choices: Transcripts delete short phrases automatically
Hedges are always spoken too quietly
Neither contains an explicit objection
items.explanation: Nothing hostile appears, so the words alone look fine.

items.prompt: After noticing a hedge, what is the next step?
choices: Assume the person is against you
Wait quietly for a follow-up to appear
Ask a short, low-stakes question
items.explanation: A short question turns the clue into information.

items.prompt: Is reading subtext the same as being paranoid?
choices: Yes, because nobody ever hides anything at all
Yes, since it assumes everyone is an enemy here
No, it treats the room as a source of information
items.explanation: It is a habit of comparing signals, not suspecting people.

items.prompt: An engineer hears 'interesting, let's sync separately' from two directors and sees one usual questioner stay silent. What does the transcript show?
choices: No objection at all, so the clues are in what replaced the expected reactions
Two approvals and one abstention that can safely be ignored by the engineer
Two rejections and one hidden supporter who is waiting for a better moment
Nothing at all, so the engineer should drop the proposal and move on right away
items.explanation: The recorded words contain nothing negative. The signals are the hedges standing in for specific questions and the pattern break, which are clues to follow up on.
items.reference:
Two common carriers of subtext
🌫️ Hedge language: sounds like agreement, commits to nothing
🤐 Silence: a reaction that was expected and did not come
❓ Both lead to the same step: ask a short question
Why: agreement that commits to nothing and a missing reaction both look harmless in a transcript, which is why they hide so much.
items.learnMore:
Hedges and silences hide in plain sight

Neither carrier contains an objection, so a transcript shows nothing wrong. They matter because of what they replace: a specific reaction that the proposal would normally have received.

Common mistake

Hearing 'interesting' or silence and recording it as approval.
items.reflection: Recall a time you answered 'sure, maybe' to avoid an argument. What were you actually protecting, and what would you have wanted the other person to ask?

items.prompt: Which pair correctly names the two carriers described in this unit?
choices: Loud disagreement, and detailed written feedback sent after the meeting
Hedge language, and silence from someone who normally reacts out loud
Calendar conflicts, and late replies from absolutely anyone on the team
Long speeches, and quick agreement from everyone sitting in the room
items.explanation: The two carriers are hedges that commit to nothing and an expected reaction that does not come.

items.prompt: Why is a hedge easier to miss than an open objection?
choices: It is spoken faster than the other sentences that people say in the room
It only appears in written messages and almost never when spoken aloud
It sounds like mild interest while committing the speaker to nothing
It always comes from a person who has little influence over the decision
items.explanation: A hedge is built to avoid conflict, so it passes for friendliness. An open objection announces itself.

items.prompt: 'Interesting' with no follow-up question usually signals what?
choices: Polite acknowledgment without endorsement
Strong enthusiasm for the whole plan
A firm commitment to fund the work
items.explanation: Real enthusiasm tends to ask something specific.

items.prompt: 'Let's take it offline' usually means what?
choices: I will not debate this here now
I will schedule a call tomorrow
The idea has been approved already
items.explanation: It defers the topic and may not lead to any follow-up.

items.prompt: 'Let me loop in someone else' can mean what?
choices: Passing the decision to another person
The decision has already been made today
The topic is now closed for good
items.explanation: Sometimes it is simple sharing, but it can pass the risk of saying no.

items.prompt: 'I'd want to think about that' often hides what?
choices: A request for more slides
Hesitation that is deferred, not stated
A signed approval to go ahead and proceed
items.explanation: It postpones a reaction that is not yet voiced.

items.prompt: Which reply shows real interest?
choices: What would the migration timeline be?
Interesting, let's see how that goes.
Noted, thanks for the update.
items.explanation: A question about the concrete plan engages with the content.

items.prompt: Is every 'interesting' a hedge?
choices: No, it can be literal
Yes, always
Only when spoken softly
items.explanation: The same words can be sincere, so context decides.

items.prompt: Besides the phrase, what else goes into a useful read?
choices: Whether a concrete next step came with it
The color of the slides in the room
How long the speaker paused for coffee
items.explanation: The missing concrete follow-up is part of the signal.

items.prompt: Who decides whether 'worth exploring' counts as approval?
choices: Nobody, it does not count as approval alone
The person who said it, in every case
Whoever happened to be the first speaker
items.explanation: It commits to nothing concrete, so it is not approval.

items.prompt: A colleague says 'worth exploring' and then asks what the migration timeline would be next quarter. Is the phrase working as a hedge?
choices: Yes, because the phrase is always a hedge in every meeting
Yes, because asking questions is just another way to stall things
No, because the colleague has now approved the whole plan fully
No, the specific timeline question shows real engagement with the plan
items.explanation: The test is the phrase plus whether something concrete came with it. A timeline question is concrete, so the phrase is only polite framing. It still falls short of approval.
items.reference:
Hedge phrase plus what is missing
🗣️ The phrase: 'worth exploring', 'let's take it offline'
❓ Is a specific question or next step attached?
✅ Yes: likely real engagement
🌫️ No: likely a hedge worth checking
Why: a hedge is a phrase standing in for a concrete reaction, so the test is whether anything concrete came with it.
items.learnMore:
The phrase alone proves nothing

'Interesting' can be sincere. Read the phrase together with whether a specific question or next step followed and whether that matches what you expected from this person.

Common mistake

Treating a phrase list as a dictionary where each phrase has one fixed meaning.
items.reflection: Think of a phrase a friend or colleague uses that can mean yes or no. What do you check to tell which one it is this time?

items.prompt: Two people both say 'interesting, let's take it offline.' One then books a thirty-minute slot; the other does not. Which statement is best?
choices: The booked slot is a concrete step, so that reply is more likely real
Both replies mean exactly the same thing because the words match each other
The second reply is certainly a refusal of the idea made in the meeting
The booking proves that the first person fully agrees with the whole plan
items.explanation: Identical words carry different weight depending on what follows. A booking raises the likelihood of real interest but does not prove full agreement, and the missing booking suggests rather than proves a hedge.

items.prompt: A teammate says 'let me loop in the platform lead.' When is this most likely a hedge?

When the teammate also asks a very detailed and specific question
items.explanation: Looping in someone with no say can be a way to avoid answering. If the person does hold the decision, it is plain routing.

items.prompt: Which reading of a phrase table is sound?
choices: Treat each phrase as a code with exactly one fixed meaning, every single time
Assume the speaker is hiding opposition whenever one of the phrases appears
Use it to spot a hedge standing in for a concrete reaction, then verify
Ignore every phrase that happens to sound positive, friendly, or encouraging
items.explanation: The table lists common patterns, not guaranteed meanings. Its use is to prompt a check.

items.prompt: When is a person's silence meaningful?
choices: When it breaks their usual pattern
Whenever they say nothing at all
Only when they happen to leave early
items.explanation: Silence matters against a known baseline.

items.prompt: What is a baseline?
choices: How someone normally reacts here
The first item on the agenda
The smallest budget line in the plan
items.explanation: A baseline is their usual way of responding.

items.prompt: Someone quiet in every meeting is quiet again. What does that tell you?
choices: Little that is truly new
That they strongly object
That they strongly agree
items.explanation: It matches their pattern, so it adds no signal.

items.prompt: A new hire at their second meeting says nothing. What can you infer?
choices: Nothing yet, there is no baseline
That they oppose the plan completely
That they already approved it fully
items.explanation: Two meetings is not enough to know a pattern.

items.prompt: The person who always asks the first hard question stays silent. This is called what?
choices: A pattern break
A routine agreement from them
A scheduling conflict in the day
items.explanation: The missing reaction breaks their known pattern.

items.prompt: Which could explain a pattern break besides opposition?
choices: They were distracted or raised it privately
They have been replaced by somebody else
The proposal was flawless by definition itself
items.explanation: Innocent explanations exist, so ask before concluding.

items.prompt: After spotting a meaningful silence, what is the next step?
choices: Ask them privately and calmly
Name them as the opponent in front of everyone
Stop the project immediately
items.explanation: A private question turns the clue into information.

items.prompt: Does a broken pattern prove opposition?
choices: No, it only suggests a question to ask
Yes, in every case where it happens
Yes, whenever the person also leaves early
items.explanation: It is a clue and not proof.

items.prompt: Priya always asks the first pointed question and says nothing for ten minutes on your proposal. Which conclusion is justified?
choices: She opposes the plan and will block it when it reaches a formal vote
She approved the plan, since she did not raise any objection in the room
The silence tells you nothing at all about her view of the whole plan
Her usual reaction is missing, so something is probably on her mind
items.explanation: A broken pattern from a known person is a signal that something exists, not what it is. Opposition and approval are both guesses, and dismissing it ignores real information.
items.reference:
Does silence tell you anything?
Usually quiet and quiet now: no new information
Usually first to push back and quiet now: pattern break, worth asking
New to the team: no baseline, so no inference
Why: silence only carries information against a known baseline for that person.
items.learnMore:
A baseline makes silence readable

Silence from someone who is quiet in every meeting says nothing new. Silence from someone who reliably reacts is a pattern break, and even then it is a prompt to ask, since distraction or a private conversation can explain it.

Common mistake

Reading meaning into the silence of someone you have barely seen react.
items.reflection: Think of someone whose silence you can read because you know them well. What do you know about them that makes it readable?

items.prompt: A person who rarely speaks stays quiet on your proposal. Which reading is best?
choices: It matches their usual pattern, so it adds no information about your plan
It shows they are secretly against the whole proposal
It shows they would certainly speak up if they objected
It shows that the group fully agrees with everything you said
items.explanation: Silence in line with a baseline is not a new signal. Treating it as opposition or consensus invents meaning.

Two meetings is plenty to know anyone's usual pattern of speaking
Silence from people who are new always means that they approve
items.explanation: A baseline needs enough observations. Two meetings cannot show whether someone is quiet by nature, new, or reserved.

choices: She cannot understand the topic of the proposal at all, so she stayed out
She has been told to stay silent by you, the person making the proposal
She raised it privately already or saves it for a smaller setting
She always agrees whenever she happens to say nothing during discussion
items.explanation: Several harmless explanations exist, which is why the right response is a question and not a conclusion.

items.prompt: After noticing a clue, which move is best?
choices: Ask a calm, low-stakes question
Confront the person in front of the group
Quietly assume the worst and stop
items.explanation: Asking gets real information without accusing anyone.

items.prompt: Which question is low-stakes?
choices: Is there a risk I should check first?
Why exactly are you blocking this plan?
Who told you to object to my idea?
items.explanation: It invites information instead of accusing.

items.prompt: Where is it best to ask?
choices: Privately
In front of the full group
By announcing it in a channel
items.explanation: A private setting avoids defensiveness.

items.prompt: If the guess was wrong, what does asking cost?
choices: Almost nothing
The whole project
A formal warning
items.explanation: A brief question costs little either way.

items.prompt: If the guess was right, what does asking usually do?
choices: Brings the concern out early
Makes the concern disappear
Starts an argument every time
items.explanation: A direct, private question often lets a real concern surface.

items.prompt: Which is a failure mode?
choices: Acting on a read as if it were confirmed
Asking a short follow-up question
Noticing a silence and wondering why
items.explanation: Treating a guess as fact skips the check.

items.prompt: Which phrase invites information from someone with more authority?
choices: I value your read. Is anything missing?
You seemed against this when we met.
I already know that you disagree here.
items.explanation: It is respectful and open, not accusing.

items.prompt: Is treating every hedge as proof of opposition a good habit?
choices: No, it burns trust on false signals
Yes, because it keeps you completely safe
Yes, since it speeds up every decision
items.explanation: Not every hedge is opposition.

items.prompt: Director B says 'I'd want to think about the cost implications.' Which follow-up best turns this into information?
choices: Are you planning to block this plan because of the cost that is involved?
Cost is not a real problem here, so can we simply continue with the plan now?
Could you send the whole team your concerns about the cost in writing, please?
When you say cost, which cost worries you most: infrastructure, maintenance, or priority?
items.explanation: The question names the one specific concern and asks which part matters, without accusing or dismissing it. The others accuse, dismiss, or turn a private clue into a public task.
items.reference:
From a read to a question
👀 Notice the clue
💬 Ask privately, in a low-stakes way
✅ Real concern surfaces early, or nothing is lost
🚫 Do not confront or act on the guess
Why: a question works whether the guess was right or wrong, while acting on the guess works only if it was right.
items.learnMore:
The question is the whole value of the read

A private, non-accusing question converts an ambiguous signal into information. If a concern exists it tends to surface, and if none exists the question cost almost nothing.

Common mistake

Skipping the question and either dropping the idea or escalating based on the guess.
items.reflection: Think of a time you assumed something about someone and later learned you were wrong. What one question would have saved you the trouble?

items.prompt: Which choice best shows why a private question beats acting on a guess?
choices: It gives you real information whether the guess was right or wrong
It lets you be certain of the other person's motives
It removes the need to read the room at any point
It works only when the person already agrees with you
items.explanation: Asking yields real information in both cases. Certainty about motives is never gained, and it is not conditional on agreement.

items.prompt: You read a colleague's silence as opposition and tell two others 'they are against this.' What went wrong?
choices: You noticed a silence, which you should never do
A guess was repeated as a fact without checking it
You asked the colleague directly too soon
You waited too long before speaking in the meeting
items.explanation: Noticing is fine. The error is acting on an unverified read and spreading it, which can harm a relationship over something never said.

items.prompt: Which reaction broke a known pattern?
choices: Director A's reply
Priya's silence
Director B's reply
items.explanation: Priya usually asks first and said nothing.

items.prompt: What does substantive mean here?
choices: Sounding very excited about the idea
Touching a concrete part of the plan
Speaking at length for several minutes
items.explanation: Substantive means concrete content.

items.prompt: Which question is a sign of engagement?
choices: Interesting, is it lunchtime?
How does this affect on-call?
Nice, thanks for the update.
items.explanation: It touches a specific part of the plan.

items.prompt: Which reaction points to the most specific next question?
choices: Director A's 'interesting'
Director B's cost comment
Nobody's reaction
items.explanation: A named concern can be turned directly into a question.

items.prompt: Should the engineer confront Priya in the room?
choices: Yes, immediately in front of everyone
No, ask her privately
Yes, by email to the whole team
items.explanation: A public confrontation turns a clue into an accusation.

items.prompt: Was the engineer's takeaway reasonable on the transcript alone?
choices: No, there was open objection throughout
Yes, nothing said was negative
No, someone refused the idea clearly
items.explanation: That is why subtext is easy to miss.

items.prompt: Which reaction carries the most concrete information to act on, and why?
choices: Priya's silence, because silence is always the loudest signal
Director A's, because it came first in the meeting
Director B's, because it names a specific concern, cost
None, because all three are hedges with equal weight
items.explanation: A named concern points at a question to ask. Silence says a concern probably exists but not what it is, and A's reply says only that nothing substantive happened.
items.reference:
Decoding the three reactions
🗣️ Director A: hedge, no content, low confidence
💬 Director B: hedge plus one named concern, cost
🤐 Priya: pattern break, content unknown
➡️ Most to act on: B's named cost concern
Why: a named concern is the most concrete thing in a hedge-heavy room, even when a silence feels louder.
items.learnMore:
Rank clues by how much they point to

A hedge with nothing under it says little. A pattern break says a concern probably exists. A hedge carrying one specific concern points straight at a question to ask.

Common mistake

Acting on whichever reaction feels most alarming instead of the one that names something.
items.reflection: In your last group discussion, which comment contained the most specific information, and was it also the loudest?

items.prompt: Director A says 'interesting, let's take it offline' and nothing else. Which read is most honest?
choices: A clear refusal that was made politely in front of all of the others there
A promise to book a meeting sometime this week with more of the details
A request for much more detail about the cost of the whole of the plan
Likely non-committal, with low confidence about what lies underneath
items.explanation: With no content under the hedge, the honest read is low confidence. It could be avoiding debate in public or genuine busyness.

items.prompt: Compare Director B and Priya. What distinguishes them?
choices: B gave a specific concern in words; Priya's silence says one exists
B opposes the plan completely, while Priya supports the plan fully instead
B has less influence than Priya has in the room when decisions are made
Both of them gave exactly the same amount of useful information to act on
items.explanation: One carries content, the other a pattern break. Neither proves a position.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes the right next step after the meeting?
choices: Continue building and wait for somebody to raise an objection later
Ask B which cost worries them and ask Priya privately about it
Tell the rest of the team that B and Priya both have doubts
Repeat the proposal to both of them until they finally agree
items.explanation: Two separate private questions convert the clues into facts. Waiting or spreading the guess skips the check.

items.prompt: When should the engineer ask their follow-up?
choices: After two weeks of building
Right after the meeting
Only if the plan fails
items.explanation: Early checks are cheap.

items.prompt: What happened in the real scenario after two weeks?
choices: It was approved in full by everyone
The proposal quietly left the agenda
It was announced by the two directors
items.explanation: No one killed it openly; it just stopped appearing.

items.prompt: With 5 working days a week, two weeks is how many working days?
items.explanation: Two weeks of five days each is ten working days.

items.prompt: Is the read less wrong if it is caught later?
choices: Yes, because it becomes correct over time
No, the read is the same; the cost is higher
Yes, since the cost disappears with the delay
items.explanation: Timing changes the cost, not whether the read was wrong.

items.prompt: Who should schedule a follow-up that matters?
choices: Whoever said 'offline'
The proposer
The quietest person in the room
items.explanation: A hedge guarantees no follow-up, so the proposer must arrange it.

items.prompt: What does a wrong read cost if asked on day 1?
choices: The whole quarter
Almost nothing
The proposer's job
items.explanation: Little has been built yet.

items.prompt: Why can a late check be worse?
choices: The people involved changed their names
Work piled up on an unverified assumption
The meeting notes got a lot shorter
items.explanation: Cost grows with what is built on the guess.

items.prompt: Which is a failure mode?
choices: Asking quickly and privately after the meeting
Waiting until the proposal disappears to ask
Noting the clue and then checking on it
items.explanation: Late checks lose the chance to adjust cheaply.

items.prompt: The engineer builds for 10 working days before learning a concern existed. Compared with asking at the end of day 1, how many more working days rested on the unverified guess?
choices: 10 more working days
5 more working days
9 more working days
1 more working day
items.explanation: Day 1 puts 1 day at risk and week 2 puts 10, so the extra exposure is 10 minus 1, which is 9 days. The guess was equally wrong both times.
items.reference:
Cost of an unchecked read (assumed 5 working days a week)
Checked at end of day 1: 1 working day built on the guess
Checked at end of week 1: 5 working days
Checked at end of week 2: 10 working days
The read can be equally wrong at each point; the cost differs
Why: the price of a wrong read rises with how much gets built on it before anyone checks.
items.learnMore:
Ask early, while changing course is cheap

A misread caught the next day costs a question. The same misread left for two weeks puts ten working days of effort into a direction nobody approved, and the decision to drop it can happen without you.

Common mistake

Waiting for a follow-up that was never going to be scheduled.
items.reflection: Think of a project where a doubt surfaced late. What would have changed if someone had asked the same question in the first week?

items.prompt: Why is the timing of a check as important as whether the read was right?
choices: Late checks turn a wrong read into a correct read as more time passes by
Early checks prove what the other person's real motive was in the meeting
Timing matters only to the people who actually spoke in the meeting itself
Cost grows with the work built before the check, while the misread stays the same
items.explanation: The same wrong read costs a question on day 1 and about two weeks of effort later. Neither timing changes the facts or reveals motives.

items.prompt: After 'let's take it offline,' no meeting appears for a week. What is the best conclusion?
choices: The phrase never guaranteed a follow-up, so book it yourself
The directors have approved the idea silently in the background
The directors are certainly against the idea and say so by silence
Nothing should be done until the directors decide to respond
items.explanation: A hedge does not promise action. If the topic matters, the proposer arranges the conversation, without assuming approval or hostility.

items.prompt: What carries over to other meetings?
choices: The exact phrases used in this room
Priya's personal habits in meetings
Noticing a hedge in place of content
items.explanation: The method travels; the details do not.

items.prompt: What is specific to this room?
choices: Hedges replace specific reactions
Silence can be a clue
Priya usually asks first
items.explanation: A baseline belongs to particular people.

items.prompt: Can the same phrase mean different things?
choices: No, never in any setting
Only when it is written down
Yes, with another speaker or team
items.explanation: Context changes meaning.

items.prompt: If Priya spoke first with enthusiasm, what changes?
choices: The directors become certain opponents
Everyone in the room has approved it
There is one real supporter in the room
items.explanation: The overall read shifts even though A and B said the same words.

items.prompt: Is this one scenario the whole territory?
choices: Yes, it covers everything
Yes, for all companies
No, it is one case
items.explanation: Changing the facts changes the right move.

items.prompt: Is announcing 'Priya opposes this' wise?
choices: Yes, it gives the team a warning
Yes, it saves everyone some time
No, it spreads a guess as a fact
items.explanation: It can damage a relationship over something never said.

items.prompt: Should phrases from this room be assumed in another company?
choices: Yes, they are universal everywhere
Yes, as long as they are polite
No, check what they mean there
items.explanation: Meaning depends on people and context.

items.prompt: What is the safest way to carry the method elsewhere?
choices: Reuse the phrase table as a fixed rulebook
Assume that silence always means approval
Relearn baselines and verify with questions
items.explanation: The method needs fresh baselines each time.

items.prompt: Priya speaks first with detailed enthusiasm, and the two directors say exactly what they said before. How does the overall read change?
choices: Both directors have now become supporters of the plan as a result of her words
One real supporter plus two hedges that still need a follow-up from you
Both directors are now shown to be opposed to the plan because of her words
The directors' words no longer matter at all to the overall read of the room
items.explanation: The directors' words are unchanged, so they still need checking. Priya adds one concrete piece of support. Supporters and opponents cannot be assumed from words that stayed the same.
items.reference:
What carries over, what does not
✅ Carries over: hedge instead of content, pattern breaks, ask before acting
🏷️ Specific to this room: exact phrases, Priya's habit of asking first
🔄 Change the facts, and the read changes
Why: the method generalizes, while the particular phrases and baselines belong to one room and can mean something else elsewhere.
items.learnMore:
A case, not the whole territory

The scenario shows a method. If Priya had spoken first with detailed enthusiasm, the same two hedges would sit in a different picture: one real supporter plus two who still need a follow-up.

Common mistake

Carrying one room's phrase meanings or baselines into a different team.
items.reflection: Pick a phrase that means something specific in your own team. Would a newcomer or another team read it the same way?

items.prompt: Which part of the meeting analysis is most likely to fail if used in a different company?
choices: Comparing a hedge with the reaction that you had expected
Asking before acting on a read of the room you are in
The exact phrases and the baseline that Priya asks first
Noticing a silence that breaks someone's usual pattern
items.explanation: Phrases and baselines are local. The method of comparing, noticing, and asking stays useful.

items.prompt: Suppose the silent person were the engineer's own manager. Which statement is most reasonable?
choices: The same read applies without any changes at all, since the room is the same
Silence from a manager always means approval of the plan being put forward
Silence from a manager can safely be ignored in every case that comes up
The baseline and the stakes differ, so rebuild the read before borrowing it
items.explanation: A manager has different stakes and a different pattern, so the read must be rebuilt from their baseline. Nothing carries over automatically.

Treat it as proof for this team too, since the phrase is the same
Discard it because phrases never carry any meaning at all
Announce it to the team as a warning about the person
items.explanation: Another room's habit is data about that room. It becomes useful here only after checking with the people in this one.
